title: The Things We Never Say
author: Mowles, Chris
summary: Elizabeth Strout's most recent novel The Things We Never Say deals with openness and secrecy in relationships, and the difficulty of talking about what's going on between people, even when we long to. In the novel the central character, Artie Dam, complains to his wife that at the neighbourhood cocktail parties they attend together, people aren't having 'real' conversations. They don't talk about what's going on in their lives despite the fact that everyone attending the party knows at least the dramatic outlines. Instead they avoid the obvious, the serious, and chatter politely about things uncontentious. And yet despite his yearning for the 'real', Artie can't tell his wife that he discovers the biggest secret she is keeping from him. He does eventually tell a relative stranger who becomes a confidant and friend. Moreover, Artie finds out that the new friend he can open up to has just voted for Trump to be president for the second time, a prospect which Artie views with complete horror. They can talk together about their relationships, unusual in men of their age, but they don't talk about politics. It never comes up. So whether we are very close to the people we would like to be straight with or not, we still have to navigate interdependencies. Amongst many other things, the novel is a long deliberation about the constant and fluctuating ethical dilemmas involved in any relationship, the trade-offs present in competing goods and possible conflicting harms. It worries away at the idealisation that in order to thrive we should always be open and honest with each other, which you often hear in organisations. It also vividly portrays how hard it is to have difficult conversations, particularly with those we are close to, but not just these. The closer the relationship, the higher the emotional stakes, but in every relationship there are comprises, silencings and negotiation with ourselves and with others . This is not to say that the opposite of idealisation is true, that we shouldn't be open with each other, and should avoid discussing the uncomfortable, but that to rub along with each other requires the exercise of practical judgement and a constant wrestling with what to conceal and what to reveal, caught up in the tensile, fluctuating dialectic of trust. This novel came to mind for me during some sessions I have attended at the Towards Relational Public Services 2026 conference , where a whole host of practitioners, academics and pracademics talked about their brilliant practical, often grassroots experiments in making public services more human. To do so they are working against the modern pathologies of marketisation, instrumentalism and competition inherent in New Public Management which drive out the relational. They are trying to bridge what citizens, communities, patients and clients really want, and what staff in public services feel they are constrained to provide. But relational public services sounds like tautology. Shouldn't public services always be thought of as relational? We are as human beings, always and already in relation. But that's not how it feels to many people for whom eligibility criteria, KPIs, outcomes, pathways, packages of care might sound like meaningless bureaucratic jargon. They know what relational public services feel like when they experience them, and certainly when they don't. In many parts of the UK public services we produce what the German sociologist Rahel Jaeggi calls a relation of relationlessness. So there is a relation, but one which can make people using public services, particularly those in most need of them, feel objectified, let down and not seen in their particularities. In not recognising their unique needs we can send citizens on a labyrinthine journey where they expereince gatekeeping and exclusion which ends up by having to treat them as an emergency later on. This is bad for everyone. Bad for the citizen looking for recognition, bad for the public sector worker on the treadmill of feeling powerless and bad for the taxpayer who ends up paying more for a firefighting approach. From the presentations I heard, there were a number of cases where citizens had not been asked systematically about what mattered to them, or if they had been, public services were unable to respond flexibly and adaptively. But entering into 'real' conversations was often the start of a process which often provoked strong emotions on all sides. In the conference we were all committed to collaborating more, which involved staff in the public services having difficult conversations with each other, and with communities But collaboration is easy to say, and difficult to do because there often involve The Things We Never Say. It is easy to get lost in high-sounding abstractions like trust, authenticity, synergy, adaptability, alignment, vision, learning, and miss the importance of power, politics, strong feelings and compromise. Talking about what's going on means making things visible which perhaps we would rather remain invisible. I attended two presentations in particular which seemed to me to be dealing with the grit of organisational change, and which were explicit about the highly political and identity-challenging nature of the work (I am sure that there were many others I was unable to attend). One was entitled What if Learning Isn't the Problem, presented by Karen MacNeil of the Phronesis Partnership and Pauline Lunn (In Control Scotland), which, amongst other things, was a highly relational account of institutional power politics. No surprise that Karen would tell me that 'everything is political', and that the project involved phronesis (nominative determinism for Karen's organisation), the entanglement of practical judgement, politics and ethics. Not everyone who tells you they want to collaborate is going to collaborate, but instead may block, obfuscate and play bureaucratic games. The other was an account by Claire Kenwood of Leeds and York NHS Partnership Trust of work she and colleagues had been doing in order to generate greater collaboration amongst different mental health teams. The title of Claire's talk was slightly misleading when it described the project as involving 'evidence-based measurement to bridge policy, practiced and improved service user outcomes'. It was indeed evidence based, but the interesting aspect of the work not revealed in the title of the workshop were the hard yards of identity work involved in the collaboration. Collaborating better also involved coming to terms with how everyone was contributing to a less helpful dynamic, including oneself, potentially othering different teams as being the guilty party. The French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu confessed to being much more interested in why things stay the same, rather than why they change. One insight shared over and over again at the TRIPS Conference is that we all know why things aren't working, and we know what needs to be done. But we are all more or less caught up in the game we are playing - we have an investment in it. Current dynamics are sustained by the power inherent in our interdependencies. Bourdieu was very clear that calling the game into question is a risky business. It makes the invisible visible and is likely to provoke strong feelings of embarrassment and shame, a hunt for scapegoats, a reversion to blaming and perhaps even denial. It is sometimes hard to acknowledge how we might ourselves have contributed to keeping an unhelpful dynamic going, particularly if it has been to our advantage to do so. 'Having difficult conversations' is easier said than done. It is a practice along with all other practices which might lead to running public services differently, and is likely to involve the capacity for critical reflexivity, noticing how we may have been part of the very dynamic we now come to critique.
